candidates.statement: BEIR assembles 18 datasets across 9 retrieval tasks, chosen for diversity of task, domain, difficulty, and annotation method.
Prior multi-dataset retrieval resources (MultiReQA, KILT) test narrower settings than needed to assess broad zero-shot generalization.
No single retrieval architecture consistently outperforms the others across all 18 BEIR datasets.
BM25 underperforms neural approaches by 7-18 points in-domain on MS MARCO yet outperforms most tested neural approaches on average out-of-domain across the 18 BEIR datasets.
This divergence suggests in-domain accuracy on a single benchmark is not a reliable predictor of zero-shot retrieval performance.
Ranking of average zero-shot performance vs. BM25 across the ten tested systems.
The best-generalizing architectures (re-ranking, late-interaction) are the most computationally expensive at inference.
There is a trade-off between zero-shot generalization and computational cost among the tested architecture families.
Term-weighting sparse methods fail to generalize; document-expansion sparse methods generalize well.
Dense bi-encoders underperform substantially under domain/task shift; DPR generalizes worst overall.
Re-ranking and late-interaction generalize best but still fail on some datasets.
TAS-B is the best-generalizing dense model tested.
The authors speculate TAS-B's generalization stems from its training setup.
TAS-B underperforms ANCE specifically where document-length preference is costly.
A controlled ablation isolating the similarity function reproduces the document-length-preference difference.
The similarity function is one identifiable source of length preference, but length preference alone does not indicate retrieval error.
Domain-adaptive fine-tuning (GenQ) helps on specialized domains and hurts on broad domains relative to its base model.
Manually completing missing relevance judgments on TREC-COVID changes systems' scores very unevenly by architecture family.
This indicates the TREC-COVID annotation pool was biased toward lexical systems' top hits.
Motivation: prior to BEIR it was unclear how retrieval models generalize outside their training domain/task.
Design rationale: datasets were selected to jointly maximize diversity of task, domain, difficulty and annotation method.
Design rationale: nDCG@10 was chosen because it is the only tested metric that handles both binary and graded relevance judgments comparably.
